Title: The Server Nobody Updated
Detail_lesson: On 1 August 2012 Knight Capital deployed new trading code to eight servers. A technician missed one. That server still carried old code that a reused configuration flag switched back on, and in 45 minutes it sent millions of unintended orders and lost the firm about 460 million dollars; it was sold within months. The SEC's findings point less at the one missed copy than at a release with no automated check that every server matched. Where does our release depend on someone remembering every step, and what would it take for a mismatch to be caught before customers find it? Name the step, then who would argue it is not worth automating.
SourceAttribution: SEC, In the Matter of Knight Capital Americas LLC (2013)

Title: One Mistyped Number
Detail_lesson: On 28 February 2017 an Amazon S3 engineer ran an established playbook to remove a few servers in one region. One input was typed wrong, far more capacity was removed than intended, and a large part of the internet that relied on S3 went down for hours. AWS's own summary did not blame the engineer: it changed the tool so it removes capacity slowly and refuses to go below a safe minimum. When something goes wrong because of a person's slip, do we fix the person or the tool? Pick one routine command or step in our work that would let a single typo do this much damage.
SourceAttribution: Amazon Web Services, Summary of the Amazon S3 Service Disruption (March 2017)

Title: Five Backups and None Worked
Detail_lesson: On 31 January 2017 a GitLab engineer, tired and fixing replication late at night, deleted data on the primary database instead of the secondary. When they turned to their backups, they found that none of the five methods they had set up was working reliably; about six hours of data was lost. GitLab streamed the recovery live and published a full, plain post-mortem. Which of our safety nets have we never actually tested by using them? Say what we would discover if we needed it tomorrow, and whether we would tell people what happened as openly.
SourceAttribution: GitLab, Postmortem of database outage of January 31 (2017)

Title: Breaking Things on Purpose
Detail_lesson: After moving to the cloud, Netflix built Chaos Monkey, a tool that randomly switched off servers in production during working hours. The point was not to cause outages but to make failure ordinary, so every team designed for it instead of hoping it would not come. It became the first of a family of tools that tested larger and larger failures. What failure do we only discover when it happens for real? Describe a small, safe way to make it happen on purpose here, and who would be nervous about trying it.
SourceAttribution: Netflix Technology Blog, The Netflix Simian Army (2011)

Title: The Post-Mortem With No Culprit
Detail_lesson: John Allspaw, then at Etsy, argued that when engineers are punished for mistakes they stop giving the details needed to understand them, so the same failure happens again. Etsy's blameless post-mortems asked what someone knew, what they saw and why the action made sense at the time, and treated the honest account as the valuable thing. Think of the last thing that went wrong on our team or project. Would the person closest to it have told the whole story without worrying? Name what we would need to change for that to be true.
SourceAttribution: John Allspaw, Blameless PostMortems and a Just Culture, Code as Craft (2012)

Title: The Game That Became Slack
Detail_lesson: Tiny Speck spent years building Glitch, an online game, and shut it down in 2012 when it failed to find enough players. The team had built an internal chat tool to coordinate their own work, and Stewart Butterfield's team turned that tool into Slack, which became far bigger than the game ever could have. Sometimes the most valuable thing a project produces is not the thing it set out to build. What have we built along the way, for our own use, that others might value more than our main product or plan? Say what it would take to take it seriously.
SourceAttribution: Stewart Butterfield, interviews on Glitch and Slack (2013-2014)

Title: Cutting Burbn Down to a Photo
Detail_lesson: Kevin Systrom and Mike Krieger's first app, Burbn, let people check in to places, make plans and post photos. Hardly anyone used most of it, but people kept sharing photos. They cut almost everything else, relaunched it as Instagram in October 2010, and passed a million users in about two months. What is the one part of our product, service or plan that people actually use? Name a feature or activity we would drop if we were brave, and who on the team would fight to keep it.
SourceAttribution: Kevin Systrom, interviews on Burbn and Instagram (2010-2012)

Title: The Camera Kodak Built First
Detail_lesson: In 1975 Kodak engineer Steve Sasson built one of the first digital cameras. He later recalled the reaction as interest, but a reluctance to pursue anything that threatened the film business that paid for everything. Others built the digital future, and Kodak filed for bankruptcy in 2012. What change could make our most profitable work matter less, and are we treating it as a threat to manage or an opportunity to own? Name one thing we are protecting that might be holding us back.
SourceAttribution: Steve Sasson, interview in The New York Times (2008); Kodak Chapter 11 filing (2012)

Title: Qwikster: Right Direction and the Wrong Way
Detail_lesson: In 2011 Netflix raised prices and announced it would split its DVD business into a separate service called Qwikster, with its own site and account. Customers were furious; Netflix lost about 800,000 US subscribers in a quarter and dropped the split within weeks. Reed Hastings later said the move to streaming was right, but he had moved too fast and explained it badly. Think of a change we are planning that we believe in. How would the people affected first hear about it, and what would make them feel it was done to them rather than for them?
SourceAttribution: Reed Hastings, Netflix blog post and letter to shareholders (2011)

Title: Selling the Plumbing
Detail_lesson: Amazon built a large amount of infrastructure to run its own shop: storage, computing, and the tooling to manage it. In 2006 it began selling that infrastructure to anyone as Amazon Web Services, starting with S3 and EC2, and it became one of the company's most profitable businesses. What do we have to be good at internally that others struggle with? Name it, then say whether offering it to others would make it better or distract us.
SourceAttribution: Amazon Web Services launch announcements for S3 and EC2 (2006)

Title: What Google Found About Teams
Detail_lesson: Google's Project Aristotle studied 180 of its own teams to find out what made some effective. The biggest factor was not talent, seniority or how the team was structured but psychological safety: whether people believed they could take a risk, ask a question or admit a mistake without being punished or embarrassed. On our team, what is one question someone might not ask because of how it would look? Say what a leader could do this month that would make asking it feel normal.
SourceAttribution: Google re:Work, Guide: Understand team effectiveness (2015); The New York Times Magazine (2016)

Title: Feed the Team With Two Pizzas
Detail_lesson: Jeff Bezos set a rule for Amazon teams: no larger than could be fed with two pizzas. The point was less about food than about communication: small teams with clear ownership move faster and need fewer meetings to agree. As teams grow, the number of people who must stay in sync grows much faster than the headcount. Where is our work slowed down by how many people must agree? Name a decision that could belong to a smaller group, and what would make the rest of us trust them with it.
SourceAttribution: Colin Bryar and Bill Carr, Working Backwards (2021)

Title: Copying the Spotify Model
Detail_lesson: In 2012 two Spotify coaches published a short paper describing squads, tribes, chapters and guilds. Companies around the world copied it. Later, people who worked at Spotify said the model was a snapshot of an aspiration, that it was never fully implemented as described, and that parts of it caused problems they had to fix. The authors themselves warned against copying it. What practice have we borrowed from another company because it worked for them? Say what problem it was solving there, and whether we actually have that problem.
SourceAttribution: Henrik Kniberg and Anders Ivarsson, Scaling Agile @ Spotify (2012); Jeremiah Lee, Spotify's Failed #SquadGoals (2020)

Title: From Know-It-All to Learn-It-All
Detail_lesson: When Satya Nadella became Microsoft's CEO in 2014, he set out to change a culture where people competed to look like the smartest person in the room. He described the goal as moving from know-it-alls to learn-it-alls, drawing on Carol Dweck's research on a growth mindset, and credited the shift with the company's recovery. In our meetings, what gets rewarded: knowing the answer, or finding it out? Name one habit we have that makes it costly to say "I don't know yet".
SourceAttribution: Satya Nadella, Hit Refresh (2017)

Title: Adequate Performance Gets a Generous Severance
Detail_lesson: In 2009 Reed Hastings published Netflix's culture deck. One of its most quoted lines said adequate performance gets a generous severance package: Netflix wanted only people it would fight to keep, and gave them unusual freedom in return. It drew admiration and criticism in equal measure, and Netflix revised it over the years. What does our team actually do about adequate performance, as opposed to what we say? Say what would change if we were as explicit about our expectations as Netflix was, and what we would lose.
SourceAttribution: Reed Hastings, Netflix Culture: Freedom and Responsibility (2009); Hastings and Erin Meyer, No Rules Rules (2020)

Title: A Phone With No Keyboard
Detail_lesson: When Apple announced the iPhone in January 2007, the leading business phones all had physical keyboards, and rivals publicly laughed at a phone without one. Apple bet that a screen which could become any interface was worth losing the feel of keys. Within a few years almost every phone looked like it. What feature do our customers say they cannot live without, which might be stopping us from offering something better? Name it, and say what evidence would convince us to take the risk.
SourceAttribution: Apple iPhone launch keynote (January 2007)

Title: Glass and the People Around It
Detail_lesson: Google Glass reached early users in 2013. The technology worked, but the people around the wearers did not want to be recorded or looked up without knowing, and bars and cinemas banned the device. Consumer sales stopped in 2015; it lived on for factory and warehouse work, where those concerns mattered less. Who is affected by what we make or do, without being our user? Name one person or group like that, and how we would find out what they think before launch.
SourceAttribution: Google Glass Explorer programme (2013-2015), contemporary reporting

Title: Tay Learned From the Wrong Teachers
Detail_lesson: In March 2016 Microsoft launched Tay, a chatbot that learned from conversations on Twitter. Within a day, a group of users deliberately taught it to post offensive messages, and Microsoft took it offline in under 16 hours. Microsoft said it had planned for many kinds of abuse but not this coordinated attack. What would someone determined to misuse our product, process or data actually do? Name one way, and who on the team would be best at thinking like them.
SourceAttribution: Microsoft, Learning from Tay's introduction (official blog, March 2016)

Title: Write the Press Release First
Detail_lesson: At Amazon, many new products start with a press release and a list of questions and answers, written before anything is built. If the team cannot explain clearly why a customer should care, the idea goes back for work, while changing it is still cheap. The document is read and argued over by leaders before any engineering starts. Take something we are about to start. Could we write its one-page announcement today, in words a customer would use? Say what would be hardest to write, and what that tells us.
SourceAttribution: Colin Bryar and Bill Carr, Working Backwards (2021)

Title: A Gigabyte on April Fool's Day
Detail_lesson: Google launched Gmail on 1 April 2004 with a gigabyte of free storage, when the big free email services offered a few megabytes. Many people assumed it was a joke. The project had started as one engineer's side project, Paul Buchheit's, years before. Its offer changed what people expected email to be, and rivals raised their limits within months. Where are we competing on small improvements when a much bolder offer might change the game? Name one, and what we would have to believe to make it.
SourceAttribution: Google press release, Google Gets the Message, Launches Gmail (April 2004)

Title: Disagree and Commit
Detail_lesson: In his 2016 letter to shareholders, Jeff Bezos described a decision where he disagreed with his team but told them to go ahead, and committed to it fully. He argued that leaders who disagree can still say "I disagree, but I'll commit" rather than slowing everything down until everyone agrees, and that this works in both directions. When we disagree on our team, what usually happens: we keep arguing, we quietly don't commit, or we commit? Name a recent decision where one of those happened.
SourceAttribution: Jeff Bezos, 2016 Letter to Amazon Shareholders

Title: One-Way and Two-Way Doors
Detail_lesson: In his 2015 letter to shareholders, Jeff Bezos split decisions into two kinds. Some are one-way doors, hard to reverse, and deserve care. Most are two-way doors: if they are wrong, you walk back through. He warned that big organisations use the slow, careful process for every decision, and lose speed for nothing. Which of our recent decisions did we treat as a one-way door when it was really two-way? Say who could make that kind of decision faster next time.
SourceAttribution: Jeff Bezos, 2015 Letter to Amazon Shareholders

Title: What Would a New CEO Do?
Detail_lesson: In 1985 Intel was losing its memory-chip business to Japanese competitors but could not bring itself to leave. Andy Grove asked Gordon Moore what a new CEO brought in by the board would do. Moore said he would get out of memories. Grove replied: why don't we walk out the door, come back in and do it ourselves? Intel moved to microprocessors. If someone new took over our team or project tomorrow, what would they stop doing straight away? Say why we have not done it already.
SourceAttribution: Andrew S. Grove, Only the Paranoid Survive (1996)

Title: Six Pages Instead of Slides
Detail_lesson: In 2004 Jeff Bezos told Amazon's senior team to stop using PowerPoint in their meetings and to write narrative memos instead, read in silence at the start. He argued that writing full sentences forces clearer thinking than bullet points, which can hide gaps in the reasoning. What important decision did we last make from slides or a quick chat? Say what question a written argument would have forced us to answer, and who on the team would resist writing it.
SourceAttribution: Jeff Bezos, email to Amazon senior team (June 2004), quoted in Working Backwards (2021)

Title: Google Tried to Prove Managers Don't Matter
Detail_lesson: Some at Google believed managers were unnecessary for engineers. Project Oxygen studied its own data to find out and found the opposite: teams with better managers did better and kept their people. The top behaviour of good managers was being a good coach; technical expertise came last of the eight. On our team, which of the things that good managers do happen reliably, and which depend on luck? Name one a manager here could start doing next week.
SourceAttribution: Google re:Work, Guide: Develop and support managers, Project Oxygen (2008-2018)

Title: The Patch That Was Not Applied
Detail_lesson: In March 2017 a fix was published for a serious flaw in Apache Struts, a widely used web framework. At Equifax it was not applied to one system. Attackers got in through that flaw in May and stayed for weeks; the personal data of about 147 million people was taken. The fix existed; the process to make sure it reached everything did not. What known problem are we living with because the fix is boring, slow or nobody's job? Name it, and whose job it would become.
SourceAttribution: US Government Accountability Office, Actions Taken by Equifax and Federal Agencies (2018)

Title: Therac-25 and the Removed Safeguard
Detail_lesson: Between 1985 and 1987 the Therac-25 radiation therapy machine gave several patients massive overdoses; some died. Earlier models had hardware interlocks that stopped dangerous settings; the Therac-25 relied on software alone, and a timing bug that appeared only when operators typed quickly let it fire at full power. The manufacturer at first insisted the machine could not be at fault. Where have we removed a safeguard because we trusted something new to do the job? Say what would happen if that new thing failed quietly.
SourceAttribution: Nancy Leveson and Clark Turner, An Investigation of the Therac-25 Accidents, IEEE Computer (1993)

Title: The Spacecraft Lost Between Two Teams
Detail_lesson: NASA's Mars Climate Orbiter was lost in September 1999 as it arrived at Mars. One team's software produced thrust data in imperial units; the navigation team's software expected metric. Each team's work was correct on its own. The mistake lived in the gap between them, and the checks that could have caught it were not done. Where does our work pass between two teams, or two systems, on an assumption nobody has written down? Name that handover and what each side believes about it.
SourceAttribution: NASA, Mars Climate Orbiter Mishap Investigation Board Phase I Report (1999)

Title: A Launch Almost Nobody Got Through
Detail_lesson: When HealthCare.gov opened on 1 October 2013, it could barely be used; reports said only a handful of people completed sign-up on the first day. A small team of engineers from technology companies was brought in, worked directly on the problems, and got it working within weeks. That effort led to the founding of the US Digital Service. When our work is in trouble, who has the authority to fix it, and who has the knowledge? Say what happens here when those are different people.
SourceAttribution: US Digital Service founding and HealthCare.gov rescue, contemporary reporting (2013-2014)

Title: One Update to Millions of Machines
Detail_lesson: On 19 July 2024 a faulty content update from CrowdStrike's security software crashed about 8.5 million Windows computers at once, grounding flights and stopping hospitals and banks. The update went to every customer at the same time. Afterwards CrowdStrike committed to rolling such updates out in stages, to a few machines first, so a fault would show before it reached everyone. What do we change for everyone at once, when we could change it for a few first? Name one, and what would stop us staging it.
SourceAttribution: CrowdStrike, Channel File 291 Root Cause Analysis (August 2024); Microsoft (July 2024)
